raw_evidence.label: The first 48-team World Cup and its new Round of 32
raw_evidence.content: 2026 is the first FIFA World Cup with 48 teams instead of 32, split into 12 groups of four. The two group winners and runners-up advance automatically, and the eight best third-placed teams fill the rest of a brand-new 32-team knockout round (the Round of 32) that did not exist in any previous men's World Cup. That single format change is why a mid-tournament forecast is unusually hard: with 12 third places competing for 8 slots and the bracket keyed to which specific groups those eight come from, the knockout pairings are not fixed until the group stage ends. The tournament is hosted across the United States, Canada and Mexico and runs to a 2026-07-19 final.

raw_evidence.label: Champion odds — Argentina 26.3% leads a steep ladder
raw_evidence.content: As of the 2026-06-18 snapshot, the model gives Argentina the best chance of lifting the trophy at 26.3%, ahead of Spain (22.2%), France (14.6%), England (9.8%), Colombia (6.2%) and Brazil (3.9%). The distribution is steep and top-heavy: the top two account for almost half of all title probability, and only 14 of the 48 teams have even a 1% chance. These are championship probabilities — the share of 100,000 simulated tournaments each team wins — and they sum to 1.000 across the field. Argentina leads not because it is guaranteed anything, but because across every plausible bracket it survives more often than anyone else.

raw_evidence.label: The bracket is a coin-flip for nine teams
raw_evidence.content: Because only the top two of each group advance automatically and the eight best third-placed teams fill the rest of the new Round of 32, qualification splits the field into two worlds. Eight teams are already all but through (reach-R32 probability of 99% or more): Argentina, Mexico, Switzerland, Canada and others. But nine teams sit on a true knife edge, with a reach-R32 probability between 40% and 60% — Senegal (58.5%), Ghana (56.7%), Turkey (54.3%), Algeria (51.5%), Bosnia & Herzegovina (48.1%) and more, for whom a single result swings the whole tournament. For those nine, the model isn't predicting so much as describing a coin still in the air.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_04: The conditional bracket — advancement is near-certain for the elite, a coin-flip mid-table ---
print("\n=== ana_04 ===")
b = adv[["team","group","p_advance_group","p_best_third","p_reach_r32"]].copy()
b = b.sort_values("p_reach_r32", ascending=False)
print("Reach-Round-of-32 probability (auto top-2 + best-third path):")
for _, r in b.head(6).iterrows():
    print(f"  {r['team']:14} grp {r['group']}  R32 {r['p_reach_r32']*100:5.1f}%  "
          f"(top2 {r['p_advance_group']*100:.0f}% + 3rd-path {r['p_best_third']*100:.0f}%)")
print("  ...mid-table coin-flips (R32 40-60%):")
mid = b[(b["p_reach_r32"]>=0.40) & (b["p_reach_r32"]<=0.60)].head(8)
for _, r in mid.iterrows():
    print(f"  {r['team']:14} grp {r['group']}  R32 {r['p_reach_r32']*100:5.1f}%")
print(f"teams essentially through (R32>=99%): {(adv['p_reach_r32']>=0.99).sum()}")
print(f"teams on a knife edge (R32 40-60%): {((adv['p_reach_r32']>=0.40)&(adv['p_reach_r32']<=0.60)).sum()}")

raw_evidence.label: The host venues and the trophy at stake
raw_evidence.content: The 2026 final will be played at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, one of 16 host venues spread across the three nations; matches also run through landmark grounds such as AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas, and Mexico City's Estadio Azteca, the only stadium to host three different men's World Cups. These are the concrete, photographable stakes the abstract probabilities resolve to.

raw_evidence.label: The first 48-team World Cup and its new Round of 32
raw_evidence.content: 2026 is the first FIFA World Cup with 48 teams instead of 32, split into 12 groups of four. The two group winners and runners-up advance automatically, and the eight best third-placed teams fill the rest of a brand-new 32-team knockout round (the Round of 32) that did not exist in any previous men's World Cup. That single format change is why a mid-tournament forecast is unusually hard: with 12 third places competing for 8 slots and the bracket keyed to which specific groups those eight come from, the knockout pairings are not fixed until the group stage ends. The tournament is hosted across the United States, Canada and Mexico and runs to a 2026-07-19 final.

raw_evidence.label: Champion odds — Argentina 26.3% leads a steep ladder
raw_evidence.content: As of the 2026-06-18 snapshot, the model gives Argentina the best chance of lifting the trophy at 26.3%, ahead of Spain (22.2%), France (14.6%), England (9.8%), Colombia (6.2%) and Brazil (3.9%). The distribution is steep and top-heavy: the top two account for almost half of all title probability, and only 14 of the 48 teams have even a 1% chance. These are championship probabilities — the share of 100,000 simulated tournaments each team wins — and they sum to 1.000 across the field. Argentina leads not because it is guaranteed anything, but because across every plausible bracket it survives more often than anyone else.
raw_evidence.code:
# ---- aggregate per-team probabilities ----
    def frac(arr):
        return np.bincount(np.ravel(arr), minlength=48) / N
    p_champ = frac(W[:, 104])
    p_final = frac(np.concatenate([W[:, 101], W[:, 102]]))
    p_sf = frac(W[:, 97:101])
    p_qf = frac(W[:, 89:97])
    p_r16 = frac(W[:, 73:89])
    p_ko = frac(np.concatenate([r32_home.ravel(), r32_away.ravel()]))    # reach R32
    p_win = fin_counts[1] / N; p_run = fin_counts[2] / N
    p_third = fin_counts[3] / N; p_fourth = fin_counts[4] / N
    p_best3 = frac(best_third_team)
    exp_pts = pts.mean(axis=0)

    base = pd.DataFrame({
        "team": teams, "group": [group_of[t] for t in teams],
        "elo": elo_arr.round(1), "fifa_rank": tdf["fifa_rank"].values,
        "squad_value_eur_m": tdf["squad_value_eur_m"].values,
        "p_win_group": p_win, "p_runner_up": p_run, "p_third": p_third,
        "p_advance_group": p_win + p_run, "p_best_third": p_best3,
        "p_reach_r32": p_ko, "p_reach_r16": p_r16, "p_reach_qf": p_qf,
        "p_reach_sf": p_sf, "p_reach_final": p_final, "p_champion": p_champ,
        "exp_group_points": exp_pts.round(3),
    }).sort_values("p_champion", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
    for c in [c for c in base.columns if c.startswith("p_")]:
        base[c] = base[c].round(4)

    base.to_csv(OUT / "advance_probs.csv", index=False, encoding="utf-8")
    base[["team", "group", "elo", "fifa_rank", "squad_value_eur_m",
          "p_reach_r16", "p_reach_qf", "p_reach_sf", "p_reach_final", "p_champion"]] \
        .to_csv(OUT / "champion_odds.csv", index=False, encoding="utf-8")

raw_evidence.label: Elo + Poisson + Monte-Carlo: a standard, transparent forecasting recipe
raw_evidence.content: The forecast uses a well-established three-step recipe rather than a proprietary black box. First, an Elo rating is fit on roughly a century and a half of international results (martj42's ~49k matches since 1872), giving each of the 48 teams a single strength number as of the snapshot. Second, the Elo difference between two teams is converted into expected goals via a Poisson goal model calibrated on post-2002 internationals. Third, a Monte-Carlo simulation plays out every remaining match and the full bracket tens of thousands of times, and the share of simulations a team wins becomes its championship probability. Elo-based football models in this family (FiveThirtyEight's Soccer Power Index, Eloratings.net) are the public benchmark for this kind of forecast, which is why the method earns reader trust only if it can be checked against what already happened.

The distribution is steep and top-heavy: the top two account for almost half of all title probability, and only 14 of the 48 teams have even a 1% chance. These are championship probabilities — the share of 100,000 simulated tournaments each team wins — and they sum to 1.000 across the field. Argentina leads not because it is guaranteed anything, but because across every plausible bracket it survives more often than anyone else.

raw_evidence.label: Elo + Poisson + Monte-Carlo: a standard, transparent forecasting recipe
raw_evidence.content: The forecast uses a well-established three-step recipe rather than a proprietary black box. First, an Elo rating is fit on roughly a century and a half of international results (martj42's ~49k matches since 1872), giving each of the 48 teams a single strength number as of the snapshot. Second, the Elo difference between two teams is converted into expected goals via a Poisson goal model calibrated on post-2002 internationals. Third, a Monte-Carlo simulation plays out every remaining match and the full bracket tens of thousands of times, and the share of simulations a team wins becomes its championship probability. Elo-based football models in this family (FiveThirtyEight's Soccer Power Index, Eloratings.net) are the public benchmark for this kind of forecast, which is why the method earns reader trust only if it can be checked against what already happened.

raw_evidence.label: Elo + Poisson + Monte-Carlo: a standard, transparent forecasting recipe
raw_evidence.content: The forecast uses a well-established three-step recipe rather than a proprietary black box. First, an Elo rating is fit on roughly a century and a half of international results (martj42's ~49k matches since 1872), giving each of the 48 teams a single strength number as of the snapshot. Second, the Elo difference between two teams is converted into expected goals via a Poisson goal model calibrated on post-2002 internationals. Third, a Monte-Carlo simulation plays out every remaining match and the full bracket tens of thousands of times, and the share of simulations a team wins becomes its championship probability. Elo-based football models in this family (FiveThirtyEight's Soccer Power Index, Eloratings.net) are the public benchmark for this kind of forecast, which is why the method earns reader trust only if it can be checked against what already happened.

raw_evidence.label: Leakage guard — a live mirror that already knows the future
raw_evidence.content: The historical results file is a live mirror that already contains the 2026 World Cup matches played AFTER the 2026-06-18 snapshot, through 2026-06-27. A naive model that trained on the whole file would secretly learn the very results it is meant to forecast — a textbook data-leakage failure. The honest discipline is to filter to matches dated before 2026-06-19 when fitting ratings, so the model never sees a game it is supposed to predict; the post-snapshot rows are reserved as an out-of-sample check, never as training input. Stating this guard openly is part of why the resulting numbers can be trusted.

raw_evidence.label: Why believe it — beats a naive baseline on 8,000 games, but only ties on these 28

On a large out-of-sample test of 8,000 historical internationals the model clearly beats a naive baseline (which just predicts the home/draw/away base rates): log-loss 0.900 versus 1.062 — about 15% lower error — and 58.8% result accuracy versus 48.7%. The honest position: the method is sound on the long run, and the early tournament has been noisy.

raw_evidence.label: Elo + Poisson + Monte-Carlo: a standard, transparent forecasting recipe
raw_evidence.content: The forecast uses a well-established three-step recipe rather than a proprietary black box. First, an Elo rating is fit on roughly a century and a half of international results (martj42's ~49k matches since 1872), giving each of the 48 teams a single strength number as of the snapshot. Second, the Elo difference between two teams is converted into expected goals via a Poisson goal model calibrated on post-2002 internationals. Third, a Monte-Carlo simulation plays out every remaining match and the full bracket tens of thousands of times, and the share of simulations a team wins becomes its championship probability. Elo-based football models in this family (FiveThirtyEight's Soccer Power Index, Eloratings.net) are the public benchmark for this kind of forecast, which is why the method earns reader trust only if it can be checked against what already happened.

raw_evidence.label: FIFA ranking vs. a results model — the headline disagreement
raw_evidence.content: The FIFA World Ranking (11 June 2026 release) is the official ladder, but it is a points system tuned for confederation balance and scheduling, not a pure win-prediction engine, so a results-trained Elo model routinely re-orders it. The most striking 2026 disagreement involves Colombia, ranked only 13th by FIFA yet given the model's fifth-highest title chance, and Norway, ranked 31st but carried into the top ten of deep-run probability — both rated well above their official ranking. The opposite case is Portugal, FIFA's 5th, which the model leaves outside its top six. Where a forecast and the official ranking part ways is the natural place for a reader to argue with the model.

raw_evidence.content: A results-trained Elo model re-orders the official FIFA ladder, and among the 14 real contenders the disagreements are sharp. The model's biggest upgrade is Norway, ranked 31st by FIFA but lifted to the 10th-best title chance (1.6%); next is Colombia, FIFA's 13th but the model's 5th pick at 6.2%, and Australia, FIFA's 27th up to 14th. In the other direction the model fades market darlings: Morocco drops from FIFA 7th to 12th, Portugal from 5th to 7th. At the very top the two systems agree — Argentina is first on both, England fourth on both. Where they part ways is where a reader has the most room to argue.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_02: FIFA ranking vs model ranking — disagreements among real contenders ---
print("\n=== ana_02 ===")
d = champ.copy()
d["model_rank"] = d["p_champion"].rank(ascending=False, method="min").astype(int)
d["rank_gap"] = d["fifa_rank"] - d["model_rank"]   # positive = model likes it MORE than FIFA
# restrict to teams the model gives a non-trivial title chance (>=1%) so the disagreement is meaningful,
# not driven by a pack of minnows tied at ~0% and last place.
contenders = d[d["p_champion"] >= 0.01].copy()
liked = contenders.sort_values("rank_gap", ascending=False).head(5)
faded = contenders.sort_values("rank_gap").head(5)
print("Among the 14 teams with >=1% title chance — model rates HIGHER than FIFA rank (gap = FIFA# - model#):")
for _, r in liked.iterrows():
    print(f"  {r['team']:14} FIFA#{int(r['fifa_rank']):>2} -> model#{int(r['model_rank']):>2}  "
          f"(+{int(r['rank_gap'])})  champ {r['p_champion']*100:.1f}%")
print("Among contenders — model rates LOWER than FIFA rank:")
for _, r in faded.iterrows():
    print(f"  {r['team']:14} FIFA#{int(r['fifa_rank']):>2} -> model#{int(r['model_rank']):>2}  "
          f"({int(r['rank_gap'])})  champ {r['p_champion']*100:.1f}%")
col = d[d["team"] == "Colombia"].iloc[0]
print(f"Colombia: FIFA #{int(col['fifa_rank'])}, model #{int(col['model_rank'])}, champ {col['p_champion']*100:.1f}% (5th)")
nor = d[d["team"] == "Norway"].iloc[0]
print(f"Norway: FIFA #{int(nor['fifa_rank'])}, model #{int(nor['model_rank'])}, champ {nor['p_champion']*100:.1f}%")
por = d[d["team"] == "Portugal"].iloc[0]
print(f"Portugal: FIFA #{int(por['fifa_rank'])}, model #{int(por['model_rank'])}, champ {por['p_champion']*100:.1f}%")

raw_evidence.label: Where the model fights the FIFA ranking
raw_evidence.content: A results-trained Elo model re-orders the official FIFA ladder, and among the 14 real contenders the disagreements are sharp. The model's biggest upgrade is Norway, ranked 31st by FIFA but lifted to the 10th-best title chance (1.6%); next is Colombia, FIFA's 13th but the model's 5th pick at 6.2%, and Australia, FIFA's 27th up to 14th. In the other direction the model fades market darlings: Morocco drops from FIFA 7th to 12th, Portugal from 5th to 7th. At the very top the two systems agree — Argentina is first on both, England fourth on both. Where they part ways is where a reader has the most room to argue.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_02: FIFA ranking vs model ranking — disagreements among real contenders ---
print("\n=== ana_02 ===")
d = champ.copy()
d["model_rank"] = d["p_champion"].rank(ascending=False, method="min").astype(int)
d["rank_gap"] = d["fifa_rank"] - d["model_rank"]   # positive = model likes it MORE than FIFA
# restrict to teams the model gives a non-trivial title chance (>=1%) so the disagreement is meaningful,
# not driven by a pack of minnows tied at ~0% and last place.
contenders = d[d["p_champion"] >= 0.01].copy()
liked = contenders.sort_values("rank_gap", ascending=False).head(5)
faded = contenders.sort_values("rank_gap").head(5)
print("Among the 14 teams with >=1% title chance — model rates HIGHER than FIFA rank (gap = FIFA# - model#):")
for _, r in liked.iterrows():
    print(f"  {r['team']:14} FIFA#{int(r['fifa_rank']):>2} -> model#{int(r['model_rank']):>2}  "
          f"(+{int(r['rank_gap'])})  champ {r['p_champion']*100:.1f}%")
print("Among contenders — model rates LOWER than FIFA rank:")
for _, r in faded.iterrows():
    print(f"  {r['team']:14} FIFA#{int(r['fifa_rank']):>2} -> model#{int(r['model_rank']):>2}  "
          f"({int(r['rank_gap'])})  champ {r['p_champion']*100:.1f}%")
col = d[d["team"] == "Colombia"].iloc[0]
print(f"Colombia: FIFA #{int(col['fifa_rank'])}, model #{int(col['model_rank'])}, champ {col['p_champion']*100:.1f}% (5th)")
nor = d[d["team"] == "Norway"].iloc[0]
print(f"Norway: FIFA #{int(nor['fifa_rank'])}, model #{int(nor['model_rank'])}, champ {nor['p_champion']*100:.1f}%")
por = d[d["team"] == "Portugal"].iloc[0]
print(f"Portugal: FIFA #{int(por['fifa_rank'])}, model #{int(por['model_rank'])}, champ {por['p_champion']*100:.1f}%")

raw_evidence.label: FIFA ranking vs. a results model — the headline disagreement
raw_evidence.content: The FIFA World Ranking (11 June 2026 release) is the official ladder, but it is a points system tuned for confederation balance and scheduling, not a pure win-prediction engine, so a results-trained Elo model routinely re-orders it. The most striking 2026 disagreement involves Colombia, ranked only 13th by FIFA yet given the model's fifth-highest title chance, and Norway, ranked 31st but carried into the top ten of deep-run probability — both rated well above their official ranking. The opposite case is Portugal, FIFA's 5th, which the model leaves outside its top six. Where a forecast and the official ranking part ways is the natural place for a reader to argue with the model.

raw_evidence.label: Money vs. merit — the most expensive squads rarely win
raw_evidence.content: Squad market value (Transfermarkt) and on-pitch strength are correlated but far from identical, and World Cup history is full of expensive squads that fell short and cheaper ones that overran them. The contrast is a recurring data-journalism hook: a forecast driven by results-based Elo will systematically disagree with a ranking driven by transfer-market wages, flagging which squads the market over- or under-values relative to their simulated chance of a deep run. In this dataset France and England carry the costliest squads (well over €1bn each), yet a results-based model can still rank a cheaper side ahead of them.

raw_evidence.label: Money vs. merit — Colombia is five times cheaper than France
raw_evidence.content: Squad market value and simulated success only loosely track each other. France carries the costliest squad in the tournament at €1.52bn and the model gives it a 44.4% chance of reaching the semi-finals — €34m of squad value per percentage point of that chance. Colombia's squad costs €302m, roughly a fifth of France's, yet the model still gives it a 25.2% semi-final chance, at just €12m per point — almost three times more efficient. The clearest bargains are Australia (€7m per semi-final point) and Colombia; the most expensive disappointments by this measure are Portugal (€74m per point) and Germany (€63m). The market pays for names; the model counts results.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_03: Money vs merit — squad value per point of deep-run probability ---
print("\n=== ana_03 ===")
m = adv.copy()
# deep-run = reach the semi-final; value efficiency = squad value (EUR m) per 1% SF chance
m = m[m["p_reach_sf"] > 0.02].copy()
m["eur_per_sf_pct"] = m["squad_value_eur_m"] / (m["p_reach_sf"] * 100)
m = m.sort_values("squad_value_eur_m", ascending=False)
print("Costliest squads and what the model gives them (reach-SF %):")
for _, r in m.sort_values("squad_value_eur_m", ascending=False).head(8).iterrows():
    print(f"  {r['team']:14} EUR{r['squad_value_eur_m']:7.1f}m  SF {r['p_reach_sf']*100:5.1f}%  "
          f"= EUR{r['eur_per_sf_pct']:6.1f}m per SF-point")
print("Best value (lowest EUR per SF-point), among real contenders:")
for _, r in m.sort_values("eur_per_sf_pct").head(6).iterrows():
    print(f"  {r['team']:14} EUR{r['squad_value_eur_m']:7.1f}m  SF {r['p_reach_sf']*100:5.1f}%  "
          f"= EUR{r['eur_per_sf_pct']:6.1f}m per SF-point")
fr = adv[adv["team"]=="France"].iloc[0]; co = adv[adv["team"]=="Colombia"].iloc[0]
print(f"France squad EUR{fr['squad_value_eur_m']:.0f}m, SF {fr['p_reach_sf']*100:.1f}%")
print(f"Colombia squad EUR{co['squad_value_eur_m']:.0f}m, SF {co['p_reach_sf']*100:.1f}%")
print(f"Colombia squad is {fr['squad_value_eur_m']/co['squad_value_eur_m']:.1f}x cheaper than France's "
      f"yet within {abs(fr['p_reach_sf']-co['p_reach_sf'])*100:.1f}pp of its SF chance")

sentences.summary: det_02: Why the bracket is a distribution, not a diagram (FIFA Annex C). Source: FIFA World Cup 2026 Regulations (Annex C, third-placed allocation) (https://digitalhub.fifa.com/m/636f5c9c6f29771f/original/FWC2026_regulations_EN.p) Facts: Annex C maps each combination of 8 qualifying third-placed groups to specific R32 slots; C(12,8) = 495 combinations are tabulated

raw_evidence.label: Why the bracket is a distribution, not a diagram (FIFA Annex C)
raw_evidence.content: FIFA Regulations Annex C specifies, in advance, exactly which Round-of-32 slot each qualifying third-placed team fills — but the assignment depends on WHICH eight of the twelve groups produce a qualifying third. There are C(12,8) = 495 such combinations, and Annex C is literally a 495-row lookup table. Until the final group standings are known, 'who you'd play in the Round of 32' is therefore itself a probability distribution over those 495 permutations rather than a single pairing. A forecast made at the second-matchday snapshot must integrate over all of them, which is precisely what a Monte-Carlo simulation does naturally.

raw_evidence.label: The bracket is a coin-flip for nine teams
raw_evidence.content: Because only the top two of each group advance automatically and the eight best third-placed teams fill the rest of the new Round of 32, qualification splits the field into two worlds. Eight teams are already all but through (reach-R32 probability of 99% or more): Argentina, Mexico, Switzerland, Canada and others. But nine teams sit on a true knife edge, with a reach-R32 probability between 40% and 60% — Senegal (58.5%), Ghana (56.7%), Turkey (54.3%), Algeria (51.5%), Bosnia & Herzegovina (48.1%) and more, for whom a single result swings the whole tournament. For those nine, the model isn't predicting so much as describing a coin still in the air.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_04: The conditional bracket — advancement is near-certain for the elite, a coin-flip mid-table ---
print("\n=== ana_04 ===")
b = adv[["team","group","p_advance_group","p_best_third","p_reach_r32"]].copy()
b = b.sort_values("p_reach_r32", ascending=False)
print("Reach-Round-of-32 probability (auto top-2 + best-third path):")
for _, r in b.head(6).iterrows():
    print(f"  {r['team']:14} grp {r['group']}  R32 {r['p_reach_r32']*100:5.1f}%  "
          f"(top2 {r['p_advance_group']*100:.0f}% + 3rd-path {r['p_best_third']*100:.0f}%)")
print("  ...mid-table coin-flips (R32 40-60%):")
mid = b[(b["p_reach_r32"]>=0.40) & (b["p_reach_r32"]<=0.60)].head(8)
for _, r in mid.iterrows():
    print(f"  {r['team']:14} grp {r['group']}  R32 {r['p_reach_r32']*100:5.1f}%")
print(f"teams essentially through (R32>=99%): {(adv['p_reach_r32']>=0.99).sum()}")
print(f"teams on a knife edge (R32 40-60%): {((adv['p_reach_r32']>=0.40)&(adv['p_reach_r32']<=0.60)).sum()}")

raw_evidence.label: The first 48-team World Cup and its new Round of 32
raw_evidence.content: 2026 is the first FIFA World Cup with 48 teams instead of 32, split into 12 groups of four. The two group winners and runners-up advance automatically, and the eight best third-placed teams fill the rest of a brand-new 32-team knockout round (the Round of 32) that did not exist in any previous men's World Cup. That single format change is why a mid-tournament forecast is unusually hard: with 12 third places competing for 8 slots and the bracket keyed to which specific groups those eight come from, the knockout pairings are not fixed until the group stage ends. The tournament is hosted across the United States, Canada and Mexico and runs to a 2026-07-19 final.

raw_evidence.label: Leakage guard — a live mirror that already knows the future
raw_evidence.content: The historical results file is a live mirror that already contains the 2026 World Cup matches played AFTER the 2026-06-18 snapshot, through 2026-06-27. A naive model that trained on the whole file would secretly learn the very results it is meant to forecast — a textbook data-leakage failure. The honest discipline is to filter to matches dated before 2026-06-19 when fitting ratings, so the model never sees a game it is supposed to predict; the post-snapshot rows are reserved as an out-of-sample check, never as training input. Stating this guard openly is part of why the resulting numbers can be trusted.

raw_evidence.label: What history says about favourites and hosts
raw_evidence.content: Across the men's World Cups from 1930 to 2022, the title has been won by a small set of nations, and pre-tournament favouritism is an imperfect guide: Brazil (5 titles) and a cluster of European sides dominate the honour roll, while heavily-backed favourites have repeatedly gone out early. Two contextual facts matter for reading a 2026 forecast. First, no men's World Cup has been won by a host nation since France in 1998, so home advantage is not destiny — and this model deliberately treats every match as neutral-venue, leaving host edge out entirely. Second, an in-form mid-ranked side beating its seeding is a familiar World Cup story, which is exactly the kind of disagreement-with-the-bookmakers the model is built to surface.

raw_evidence.label: Two confederations own 94% of the title chance
raw_evidence.content: The title race is geographically narrow. European (UEFA) teams hold a combined 56.4% of all championship probability and South American (CONMEBOL) teams another 37.9% — together 94.2% of the entire field's title chance. The remaining four confederations split the last 5.8% between them: Asia (AFC) 2.8%, Africa (CAF) 1.5%, North/Central America (CONCACAF) 1.4%, and Oceania (OFC) effectively 0%. Every one of the model's top six is European or South American. The 48-team field is the broadest ever, but the favourites still come from the same two continents that have won every men's World Cup.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_05: Confederation concentration at the top ---
print("\n=== ana_05 ===")
tdf = pd.read_csv(DATA / "teams.csv", encoding="utf-8")[["team","confederation"]]
cc = champ.merge(tdf, on="team")
conf = cc.groupby("confederation")["p_champion"].sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
print("Total championship probability by confederation:")
for k, v in conf.items():
    print(f"  {k:9} {v*100:5.1f}%")
uefa = conf.get("UEFA",0); conmebol = conf.get("CONMEBOL",0)
print(f"UEFA + CONMEBOL = {(uefa+conmebol)*100:.1f}% of all title probability")
print(f"top-6 confederations represented in title top-6: "
      f"{cc.sort_values('p_champion',ascending=False).head(6)['confederation'].tolist()}")

  UEFA       56.4%
  CONMEBOL   37.9%

  CONCACAF    1.4%
  OFC         0.0%
UEFA + CONMEBOL = 94.2% of all title probability

raw_evidence.label: The first 48-team World Cup and its new Round of 32
raw_evidence.content: 2026 is the first FIFA World Cup with 48 teams instead of 32, split into 12 groups of four. The two group winners and runners-up advance automatically, and the eight best third-placed teams fill the rest of a brand-new 32-team knockout round (the Round of 32) that did not exist in any previous men's World Cup. That single format change is why a mid-tournament forecast is unusually hard: with 12 third places competing for 8 slots and the bracket keyed to which specific groups those eight come from, the knockout pairings are not fixed until the group stage ends. The tournament is hosted across the United States, Canada and Mexico and runs to a 2026-07-19 final.

raw_evidence.label: Elo + Poisson + Monte-Carlo: a standard, transparent forecasting recipe
raw_evidence.content: The forecast uses a well-established three-step recipe rather than a proprietary black box. First, an Elo rating is fit on roughly a century and a half of international results (martj42's ~49k matches since 1872), giving each of the 48 teams a single strength number as of the snapshot. Second, the Elo difference between two teams is converted into expected goals via a Poisson goal model calibrated on post-2002 internationals. Third, a Monte-Carlo simulation plays out every remaining match and the full bracket tens of thousands of times, and the share of simulations a team wins becomes its championship probability. Elo-based football models in this family (FiveThirtyEight's Soccer Power Index, Eloratings.net) are the public benchmark for this kind of forecast, which is why the method earns reader trust only if it can be checked against what already happened.

raw_evidence.content: 2026 is the first FIFA World Cup with 48 teams instead of 32, split into 12 groups of four. That single format change is why a mid-tournament forecast is unusually hard: with 12 third places competing for 8 slots and the bracket keyed to which specific groups those eight come from, the knockout pairings are not fixed until the group stage ends. The tournament is hosted across the United States, Canada and Mexico and runs to a 2026-07-19 final.

raw_evidence.label: Elo + Poisson + Monte-Carlo: a standard, transparent forecasting recipe
raw_evidence.content: The forecast uses a well-established three-step recipe rather than a proprietary black box. First, an Elo rating is fit on roughly a century and a half of international results (martj42's ~49k matches since 1872), giving each of the 48 teams a single strength number as of the snapshot. Second, the Elo difference between two teams is converted into expected goals via a Poisson goal model calibrated on post-2002 internationals. Third, a Monte-Carlo simulation plays out every remaining match and the full bracket tens of thousands of times, and the share of simulations a team wins becomes its championship probability. Elo-based football models in this family (FiveThirtyEight's Soccer Power Index, Eloratings.net) are the public benchmark for this kind of forecast, which is why the method earns reader trust only if it can be checked against what already happened.

raw_evidence.content: 2026 is the first FIFA World Cup with 48 teams instead of 32, split into 12 groups of four. That single format change is why a mid-tournament forecast is unusually hard: with 12 third places competing for 8 slots and the bracket keyed to which specific groups those eight come from, the knockout pairings are not fixed until the group stage ends. The tournament is hosted across the United States, Canada and Mexico and runs to a 2026-07-19 final.

raw_evidence.label: The first 48-team World Cup and its new Round of 32
raw_evidence.content: 2026 is the first FIFA World Cup with 48 teams instead of 32, split into 12 groups of four. The two group winners and runners-up advance automatically, and the eight best third-placed teams fill the rest of a brand-new 32-team knockout round (the Round of 32) that did not exist in any previous men's World Cup. That single format change is why a mid-tournament forecast is unusually hard: with 12 third places competing for 8 slots and the bracket keyed to which specific groups those eight come from, the knockout pairings are not fixed until the group stage ends. The tournament is hosted across the United States, Canada and Mexico and runs to a 2026-07-19 final.

raw_evidence.label: Elo + Poisson + Monte-Carlo: a standard, transparent forecasting recipe
raw_evidence.content: The forecast uses a well-established three-step recipe rather than a proprietary black box. First, an Elo rating is fit on roughly a century and a half of international results (martj42's ~49k matches since 1872), giving each of the 48 teams a single strength number as of the snapshot. Second, the Elo difference between two teams is converted into expected goals via a Poisson goal model calibrated on post-2002 internationals. Third, a Monte-Carlo simulation plays out every remaining match and the full bracket tens of thousands of times, and the share of simulations a team wins becomes its championship probability. Elo-based football models in this family (FiveThirtyEight's Soccer Power Index, Eloratings.net) are the public benchmark for this kind of forecast, which is why the method earns reader trust only if it can be checked against what already happened.

raw_evidence.label: Money vs. merit — the most expensive squads rarely win
raw_evidence.content: Squad market value (Transfermarkt) and on-pitch strength are correlated but far from identical, and World Cup history is full of expensive squads that fell short and cheaper ones that overran them. raw_evidence.label: The first 48-team World Cup and its new Round of 32
raw_evidence.content: 2026 is the first FIFA World Cup with 48 teams instead of 32, split into 12 groups of four. The two group winners and runners-up advance automatically, and the eight best third-placed teams fill the rest of a brand-new 32-team knockout round (the Round of 32) that did not exist in any previous men's World Cup. That single format change is why a mid-tournament forecast is unusually hard: with 12 third places competing for 8 slots and the bracket keyed to which specific groups those eight come from, the knockout pairings are not fixed until the group stage ends. The tournament is hosted across the United States, Canada and Mexico and runs to a 2026-07-19 final.

raw_evidence.label: Elo + Poisson + Monte-Carlo: a standard, transparent forecasting recipe
raw_evidence.content: The forecast uses a well-established three-step recipe rather than a proprietary black box. First, an Elo rating is fit on roughly a century and a half of international results (martj42's ~49k matches since 1872), giving each of the 48 teams a single strength number as of the snapshot. Second, the Elo difference between two teams is converted into expected goals via a Poisson goal model calibrated on post-2002 internationals. Third, a Monte-Carlo simulation plays out every remaining match and the full bracket tens of thousands of times, and the share of simulations a team wins becomes its championship probability. Elo-based football models in this family (FiveThirtyEight's Soccer Power Index, Eloratings.net) are the public benchmark for this kind of forecast, which is why the method earns reader trust only if it can be checked against what already happened.

raw_evidence.label: The first 48-team World Cup and its new Round of 32
raw_evidence.content: 2026 is the first FIFA World Cup with 48 teams instead of 32, split into 12 groups of four. The two group winners and runners-up advance automatically, and the eight best third-placed teams fill the rest of a brand-new 32-team knockout round (the Round of 32) that did not exist in any previous men's World Cup. That single format change is why a mid-tournament forecast is unusually hard: with 12 third places competing for 8 slots and the bracket keyed to which specific groups those eight come from, the knockout pairings are not fixed until the group stage ends. The tournament is hosted across the United States, Canada and Mexico and runs to a 2026-07-19 final.

raw_evidence.label: Elo + Poisson + Monte-Carlo: a standard, transparent forecasting recipe
raw_evidence.content: The forecast uses a well-established three-step recipe rather than a proprietary black box. First, an Elo rating is fit on roughly a century and a half of international results (martj42's ~49k matches since 1872), giving each of the 48 teams a single strength number as of the snapshot. Second, the Elo difference between two teams is converted into expected goals via a Poisson goal model calibrated on post-2002 internationals. Third, a Monte-Carlo simulation plays out every remaining match and the full bracket tens of thousands of times, and the share of simulations a team wins becomes its championship probability. Elo-based football models in this family (FiveThirtyEight's Soccer Power Index, Eloratings.net) are the public benchmark for this kind of forecast, which is why the method earns reader trust only if it can be checked against what already happened.

raw_evidence.label: Money vs. merit — the most expensive squads rarely win
raw_evidence.content: Squad market value (Transfermarkt) and on-pitch strength are correlated but far from identical, and World Cup history is full of expensive squads that fell short and cheaper ones that overran them. The contrast is a recurring data-journalism hook: a forecast driven by results-based Elo will systematically disagree with a ranking driven by transfer-market wages, flagging which squads the market over- or under-values relative to their simulated chance of a deep run. In this dataset France and England carry the costliest squads (well over €1bn each), yet a results-based model can still rank a cheaper side ahead of them.

raw_evidence.label: The host venues and the trophy at stake
raw_evidence.content: The 2026 final will be played at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, one of 16 host venues spread across the three nations; matches also run through landmark grounds such as AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas, and Mexico City's Estadio Azteca, the only stadium to host three different men's World Cups. The prize is the FIFA World Cup Trophy — the 36.8 cm gold figure of two players holding up the Earth, designed by Silvio Gazzaniga and first awarded in 1974 — which the winner lifts on 2026-07-19. These are the concrete, photographable stakes the abstract probabilities resolve to.
